original_summary: 3Up 3Down is a shedding card game for 2 to 6 players. Each player has hidden blind cards, face-up cards and a hand, and on each turn plays a card equal to or higher than the top of the discard pile, or else picks the whole pile up. Clear cards and runs of three wipe the pile, and the first player to get rid of every card wins.

review.evidence: In the original, the blind 3DOWN flips and the random refills from the draw pile are pure chance. In the previous variation, no simple policy dominated. Always picking up never sheds a card. Always playing the highest card strands low cards. Playing the lowest legal rank is competent but loses to timed forcing plays. However, First wins every race in which the players need the same number of plays, because the END CHECK ends the game immediately and First moves first. The '1' handicap costs First an extra play in only about 24% of deals (expected cost about 0.24 plays). That is a built-in seat edge.

The original is dominated by the draws: blind flips and refills. The previous variation removed the draw pile and stratified the deal, which made skill matter: choosing the Up pile, saving the Clear, and forcing a pickup with a 9 or a triple at the right moment. But the seat edge decides close races regardless of skill.

A player needs about 7.9 plays with no pickups. The quality of play shows in when you dump low groups, when you block the next seat, and when you spend the Clear, so strong players keep finding improvements. Weak but legal play still sheds cards and can win when an opponent is forced into a big pickup.

Each hand is private, but the history of plays and the known 30-card deck let players infer what an opponent can still play. Up piles are public commitments. Timing a block or a Clear needs a plan over several turns and a prediction of the next seat's reply.
Legality, run counts, clears, card counts and the winner all follow by arithmetic from the recorded plays.

The original has 2 to 6 players, a draw pile, blind flips and multi-play Clear+1 and Clear+2 cards. These are heavy, but the previous variation trimmed them to fit. That variation's claim of 15 steps per round was not broken down, and its immediate mid-round win check costs a check after every turn.

problems: Seat edge: the game ends the instant a player empties, so First wins every race in which players need equal numbers of plays, and with 7 to 9 plays needed such ties are common.

The compensation for First (an extra '1') is nearly free: it costs a play in only about 24% of deals, and it can even complete a run of three 1s and clear the Pile, so it does not offset the tempo edge.
When several players finish level, nothing decided by skill separates them; the result falls to seat order alone.
The step budget was asserted rather than shown, and an end check after every individual turn inflates the step count.

changes.what: Every player always gets the same number of turns. The win check happens once, at the end of each round, after all three players have acted. A player who empties mid-round simply passes on their remaining turns that round, and the others still take their turns.
changes.why: Moving first no longer lets a player finish a turn ahead of an equally fast opponent. A player who needs the same number of plays as First now finishes in the same round.
changes.fixes: Seat edge: the game ends the instant a player empties, so First wins every race in which players need equal numbers of plays, and with 7 to 9 plays needed such ties are common.

changes.what: Remove the extra '1' handicap card. Each player gets exactly 3 Low, 3 Mid, 3 High and 1 Clear, which uses all 30 cards.
changes.why: Once turns are equalised, no compensation is needed, and the handicap only created a new asymmetry of its own.
changes.fixes: The compensation for First (an extra '1') is nearly free: it costs a play in only about 24% of deals, and it can even complete a run of three 1s and clear the Pile, so it does not offset the tempo edge.

changes.what: If two or three players empty in the same round, the one who picked up the fewest cards over the whole game wins. If they are still tied, the game is a draw. The engine keeps a public 'cards picked up' count for each player.
changes.why: Ties in the race are settled by play quality, since avoiding pickups and forcing them on others is the core skill, not by seat.
changes.fixes: When several players finish level, nothing decided by skill separates them; the result falls to seat order alone.

changes.what: The step budget is laid out explicitly. Per round: 1 talk poll and 1 reveal. Per player: 1 choice, 1 apply step (play or pickup, using if-conditions) and 1 run/clear step. Then 1 end check and 1 cap check. That is 13 steps and 4 choice steps per round.
changes.why: This makes the build verifiable within the 20-step and 4-choice limits.
changes.fixes: The step budget was asserted rather than shown, and an end check after every individual turn inflates the step count.

keeps: Shedding by playing a rank equal to or higher than the top of the Pile, or else taking the whole Pile.
Playing several copies of one rank together, and runs of three of the same rank clearing the Pile.
Clear cards that wipe the Pile whatever is on it.
A chosen face-up Up pile, played only after the Hand is empty.
The goal: be the first to get rid of all your cards.

recommendation.reason: The shedding core already rewards inference and timing. The only failing was the tempo edge, which equal turns per round and a skill-based tiebreak remove without changing the game's identity.

variation.name: Three Up: Even Rounds
variation.summary: A three-player shedding game in which every player plays a card equal to or higher than the top of a shared Pile or else takes the Pile. Clears and runs of three wipe the Pile. All three players get equal turns, the win is checked at the end of each round, and players who finish together are separated by who picked up fewer cards.
variation.rules:
CARDS. There are 30 cards: three copies each of ranks 1 to 9 (27 cards) and three Clear cards.

SETUP.
1. Seat the three players in a random order called First, Second and Third. Turn order is First, Second, Third in every round.
2. Make three separately shuffled stacks: Low (all 1s, 2s and 3s; 9 cards), Mid (all 4s, 5s and 6s; 9 cards) and High (all 7s, 8s and 9s; 9 cards).
3. Deal each player 3 cards from Low, 3 from Mid, 3 from High and 1 Clear, so each player has 10 cards. Every card is dealt.
4. Each player privately looks at their cards.
5. At the same moment, each player chooses exactly 3 of their cards to be their Up pile. All Up piles are then revealed.
6. A player's remaining 7 cards are their Hand, which only that player sees.
7. The discard Pile starts empty, with a run count of 0. Each player's 'picked up' count starts at 0.

PUBLIC INFORMATION. At all times everyone can see:
- every card on the Pile, its top rank and its run count (how many cards of the top rank lie on top of the Pile in a row);
- every Up pile;
- each player's number of Hand cards;
- each player's picked-up count;
- the full history of plays and pickups.

EACH ROUND (at most 40 rounds).
(a) TALK. Every player writes one short message at the same moment without seeing the others. All messages are then shown to everyone. Messages bind no one.
(b) TURNS. First, then Second, then Third each take one turn as described below. A player who already has no cards in Hand or Up pile skips their turn.
(c) END CHECK. After Third's turn, look at every player who now has no cards in Hand or Up pile.
- If exactly one player is out of cards, that player wins.
- If two or three players are out of cards, the one among them with the lowest picked-up count wins. If they are tied on that count, the game is a draw.
- If nobody is out of cards, play continues.
(d) ROUND CAP. If round 40 ends with nobody out of cards, the player with the fewest cards (Hand plus Up pile) wins. A tie for fewest cards is broken by the lowest picked-up count. If players are still tied, the game is a draw.

A TURN. The player chooses one of two actions.
- PLAY: choose one rank and play one or more cards of that rank together, all from the same source.
  - The source must be your Hand while your Hand has any cards. You play from your Up pile only once your Hand is empty.
  - A numbered play is legal only if the Pile is empty or the rank is equal to or higher than the Pile's top rank.
  - A Clear is always legal and is played on its own.
- PICK UP: take every card on the Pile into your Hand, and add the number of cards taken to your picked-up count. The Pile becomes empty with a run count of 0. You may pick up even when you have a legal play. Picking up an empty Pile does nothing.
- An illegal or unreadable choice counts as PICK UP.

RESOLVING A PLAY.
- Numbered cards go on top of the Pile. If their rank equals the previous top rank, the run count rises by the number of cards played; otherwise the run count becomes the number of cards played.
- If the run count reaches 3 or more, the Pile is cleared: its cards are removed from the game, it becomes empty, and the run count is 0.
- A played Clear and the whole Pile are removed from the game, leaving the Pile empty.
- The turn then ends, and the next player acts on whatever Pile remains. An empty Pile accepts any card.
variation.objective: At the end of each round, if exactly one player has no cards left in Hand or Up pile, that player wins. If several players emptied by the end of the same round, the one with the lowest total of cards picked up during the game wins; if they are tied on that total, the game is a draw. If round 40 ends with nobody out of cards, the player with the fewest remaining cards wins, ties are broken by the lowest picked-up total, and a remaining tie is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Equal turns per round remove First's tempo win: two players who need 8 plays each now finish in the same round, and the one who absorbed fewer pickups wins. This makes forcing pickups on others, and avoiding them yourself, decisive in close races, instead of seat order. Always picking up loses to everything. Always playing the highest card strands low cards. The lowest-legal-rank heuristic loses to timed blocks with a 9 or a triple and to a well-saved Clear. Talk earns its place because only one player can win. The two trailing players can propose to gang up on the leader (for example, 'both play high so the leader must pick up'), but each also wants the other to absorb the cost of blocking. A player who follows a proposal can therefore spend their own high cards or their Clear while the proposer sheds freely, and lose. Players must judge which proposals serve the speaker. Remaining asymmetries, such as First's opening on an empty Pile and Third seeing the round's earlier plays, recur cyclically and are small. Seat win rates should still be confirmed by simulation.

balanced.evidence:
DEAL: the deal is stratified, so every player gets 3 Low, 3 Mid, 3 High and 1 Clear. The only built-in asymmetries are seat order and First's extra '1'.

TURNS NEEDED TO SHED: each PLAY sheds one rank group from one source. For a 3-card band dealt from {x,x,x,y,y,y,z,z,z} there are C(9,3)=84 hands:
| band shape | hands | distinct ranks |
|---|---|---|
| all same | 3 | 1 |
| pair + single | 54 | 2 |
| all different | 27 | 3 |
Expected distinct ranks per band = (3*1 + 54*2 + 27*3)/84 = 2.29. A player therefore needs about 2.29*3 + 1 (Clear) = 7.9 plays with no pickups.

THE HANDICAP IS MOSTLY FREE: the extra '1' costs First a play only when First holds no other 1. P(no 1 among 3 Low cards) = C(6,3)/C(9,3) = 20/84 = 24%. In 76% of deals it joins an existing group of 1s at zero extra turns. With two 1s it becomes three 1s, which reaches a run of 3 and clears the Pile. Expected cost is about 0.24 plays.

THE TEMPO EDGE IS LARGER: First moves first in every round, so in any race where players need the same number of plays, First empties first and wins under the END CHECK. First also opens on an empty Pile and can dump its least sheddable low group. With required plays clustered around 7–9, ties in play count are common, and First wins all of them. The labelled 'handicap' does not offset move order, so First has a systematic seat edge. Random seat assignment does not fix this: it only moves the edge to whoever draws First.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, under the winner rule:
- Always PICK UP: never sheds, never wins, never draws. It loses to everything.
- Always play the highest legal card: it strands low cards, which are playable only on an empty or low Pile, so it loses to sensible play.
- Always play the lowest legal rank (max copies), Clear when blocked, pick up otherwise: this is a competent shedding heuristic. It still loses to a player who plays a 9 or a triple to force the next seat into a pickup at the right moment, and to one who saves Clear.
No policy found that never loses, and no option is strictly dominant. All three players can realistically win.

The failure is the seat imbalance from a near-costless compensation.
balanced.verdict_reason: First-player tempo outweighs a handicap that costs nothing 76% of the time.

playable.evidence:
RULES ARE COMPLETE: they define legal play (rank >= top or empty Pile, Clear always legal and alone), the source rule (Up pile only when Hand is empty), multi-copy plays, run-count updates, clearing at run >= 3, Clear removal, pickup at any time, and that illegal or unreadable input counts as PICK UP. They also give an immediate win check after every turn, a 40-round cap, a fewest-cards tiebreak and a draw on ties. The game is finite and decided by arithmetic on tracked counts.

SUPPORTED FEATURES: hidden_hands, simultaneous Up-pile selection at setup, and sequential turns are all supported. There is no board, clock or judge.

BUDGET:
- Attributes: per-player Hand list, Up list and count (9), plus Pile list, top rank, run count, round and First. That is about 14, which is at most 20.
- Hidden elements: hands only, so 1, which is at most 3.
- Choice steps: talk plus 3 turns = 4, which is at most 4.
- Random draws: shuffling happens only at setup, so 0 per round.
- Steps: per turn about 4 steps (choose; compute legality flag; apply play, clear or pickup with per-operation `if`; end check with `when`). That gives 3*4 + talk = 13–15, which is at most 20. This is tight but feasible. If the engine cannot bundle conditional operations into one step, the budget breaks, so implementers should verify.

TALK: talk is simultaneous. With three players there is genuine conflict. Each player wants the next seat stuck, and two trailing players can propose to starve the leader by holding Clears or high cards. Following a proposal can cost you, so talk has content.

The repeated-game cooperation clause does not apply; this is a race, not a cooperation dilemma.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
INFERENCE IS POSSIBLE: the stratified deal, the public Up piles, card counts and full play/pickup history let a player deduce opponents' remaining ranks with high precision. The full deck composition is known, your own 10 cards are known, and each opponent holds exactly 3/3/3 per band minus what they have shown.

INFERENCE CAN BE ACTED ON:
- Play a 9 or a triple when you infer the next seat lacks a Clear or a matching rank, forcing a pickup.
- Hold your Clear until the Pile is large.
- Choose an Up pile that will be playable late.
- Time dumping low groups onto empty Piles.

CHANCE: it enters through rank shape (pairs and triples, about 3.6% for a natural triple per band) and the random First seat. Estimated chance share is about 30–40%.

WITH EQUAL GOOD PLAY: the result is not fixed by the deal, because pickups forced by opponents dominate shedding speed and good players exploit them. The random seat edge noted under balanced is the main luck component; it disappears once that check is fixed.

A reasoning player is clearly favoured over a heuristic one.

required_changes: Balanced: make First's compensation actually cost a turn. For example, make the handicap a distinct 'Lone 1' that must be played alone from Hand, never joins a group or a run, and is legal only on an empty Pile or a top of 1. This costs First about one extra play in every deal instead of 24% of deals.

Balanced (alternative or extra): give the last seat a compensating benefit, such as winning fewest-card ties against First at the round cap or receiving a second Clear in place of a High card. Then show by worked race counts or simulation that the three seats win at roughly equal rates.
Playable (safeguard): document per-turn step use, aiming for at most 4 steps per turn using per-operation `if` conditions, so the 15-steps-per-round claim is verifiable within the 20-step limit.

balanced.evidence:
SETUP SYMMETRY. Every player gets 3 Low, 3 Mid, 3 High and 1 Clear, so nobody can be dealt all the high cards or all the Clears. Each player knows their own 10 cards and every Up pile, so all three start with the same information.

SEAT EDGE. First opens on an empty Pile and may play anything. Second and Third usually face a raised top rank. The END CHECK runs only after Third's turn, so First cannot win a round before the others have acted. If two or more players empty in the same round, the lowest picked-up count wins, not seat order. Some edge remains: First is less likely to be forced to pick up in round 1, while Third has the last move before the end check. Neither is decisive, and the random seating spreads it out.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES under the winner rule:
(1) Always PICK UP. Hand size never falls; the player only gains cards. They cannot be the first to empty, and they hold the most cards at the round-40 cap. Loses to any opponent who plays.
(2) Always play the lowest legal group (the 'first option'). This is a sensible baseline, but it never forces anyone. Opponents can answer each low card cheaply and save 9s and their Clear to raise the top rank just before this player acts. When this player has only low cards left facing a high top rank, they must pick up or play their Clear. They also lose any race they are dealt a worse hand for. Typical hands are 7 to 9 rank groups; a dealt pair or triple saves a turn. So this policy loses some games against sensible play and wins some against random play: not never-losing.
(3) Always play the highest legal group (the 'last option'). Dumping 9s early leaves a 9 on top. The next players need a 9 or a Clear, or they pick up. Once the dumper has spent their 9s and Clear, they are stuck with low cards facing whatever the others raise to. They pick up repeatedly and fall behind. This loses to sensible play.
(4) Always play Clear first. This wastes the only card that rescues you from a high top rank. Later the player is forced to pick up.

DOMINANCE. No action is better whatever the opponents do:
- Playing beats picking up when you can shed safely.
- A voluntary pickup can be right when it is a cheap pickup of a small Pile, it saves your Clear, and it keeps your rank groups intact.
- Holding high cards and the Clear is valuable, but holding too long costs turns in the race.

CAN EACH SEAT WIN? Yes. With 30 cards, 3 Clears and run-of-3 clears, cards leave the game steadily. A minimum race is about 7 to 10 turns, well under 40 rounds. Every seat has realistic winning lines.

There is no labelled payoff ordering to check. The game is a shedding race decided by emptying first, with picked-up count as the tiebreak.

playable.evidence:
COMPLETENESS. The rules cover every situation:
- Legal plays: rank at or above the top rank, or an empty Pile.
- Source: Hand first, then the Up pile.
- Clear: always legal and played alone.
- Run count update and the clear at 3 or more.
- Pickup: Pile into Hand, picked-up count increases, Pile reset.
- An illegal or unreadable choice counts as PICK UP.
- Skipping a player with no cards left.
- End check after each round, the round-40 cap, and every tiebreak.
A player playing from the Up pile who then picks up gets Hand cards again, and the 'Hand first' rule covers that. The Pile never holds a Clear, so 'top rank' is always a number.

FINITENESS. The game has at most 40 rounds. The winner comes from card counts and picked-up counts, which the game keeps.

LIMITS. Steps per round: 13 of 20 allowed. Choice steps per round: 4 of 4 (one talk step plus three turns); the one-time Up-pile choice is setup. Attributes: 11 of 20 (per player Hand, Up pile and picked-up count, plus Pile and run count). Hidden elements: 1 of 3 (private hands). Random draws per round: 0 (shuffling and dealing happen once at setup). Rounds: 40. No board, judge or real clock is needed. All Up-pile choices are made at the same moment, and turns are properly sequential.

TALK. Simultaneous talk fits here. Interests conflict: the two trailing players gain by agreeing to raise the top rank against the leader, while each would rather the other spend their 9s and Clear. Following a proposal therefore costs something, and the talk is about real inference such as who still holds a Clear and who holds 9s.

This is not a fixed-length repeated cooperation game, so the late-round betrayal test does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
CHANCE. The chance elements are the seat order and which ranks you get within each band. That decides how many pairs and triples you hold, and so your minimum number of turns: roughly 7 to 10 groups, with a spread of about 2 turns. The stratified deal and the guaranteed Clear limit this variance.

REASONING. Skill matters in several ways:
- Choosing the Up pile: keep flexible or high cards there, or a pair.
- Timing the 9s and the Clear.
- Deliberately building runs of 3 to clear a Pile.
- Choosing cheap voluntary pickups.
- Inferring opponents' hands. All cards are dealt and the full history and Up piles are public, so card counting is exact. Each player knows which 20 cards the two opponents hold between them, and that set narrows as play goes on.
- Pressuring the leader through coordination at talk.

GOOD PLAY ON ALL SIDES. When everyone plays well, the deal gives a starting edge. Interaction (forced pickups, run clears, Clear timing) can swing the result by several cards, which outweighs a 1 to 2 turn advantage from the deal. Picked-up count breaks same-round ties, and it rewards skill.

I estimate chance at about 25 to 35 percent of the outcome. A player who reasons well should clearly beat a greedy or random player.
